title: About
text:
Hi, I’m a neuroscientist studying how the brain encodes, learns, and adapts. My current work is on the Cell Types & Learning project at Allen Institute / Neural Dynamics, linking spatial transcriptomics to in vivo neuronal activity during task learning.
Increasingly, that work involves developing algorithms for data acquisition, processing, and QC, deploying pipelines to scale, and building ML and agentic AI methods to make sense of large-scale, multimodal neuroscience data.
Recent focus areas:

In vivo two-photon imaging, spatial transcriptomics, multimodal data integration (neuronal activity, behavior, gene expression profile)
Role of inhibitory interneurons in sensory perception and learning
Building image data processing, QC, and analysis pipelines
GCaMP8 transgenic mice validation and characterization
Agentic AI-assisted pipeline development

Previously:

Postdoctoral research @ University of Southern California (Hires Lab): Tactile shape perception and learning
PhD research @ Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST; Dr. Yong Jeong’s lab): Neurovascular coupling in Alzheimer’s disease
Master’s research @ KAIST: Mitochonrial signaling in ROS-induced necrotic cell death
Undergraduate research @ KAIST: Nonlinear interdependence in EEGs of PTSD patients

title: Automated volumetric multimodal coregistration, Part 2: adapting to pan-neuronal expression
text: In Part 1 the pipeline was built and tested on pan-inhibitory samples. Here I apply it to pan-neuronal samples, where GCaMP is expressed in essentially all neurons. This post covers what had to change.

title: Automated volumetric multimodal coregistration, Part 2: adapting to pan-neuronal expression
text:
1. Pan-inhibitory vs pan-neuronal
Within the same 400 x 400 x 400 um volume, there are about 1,000 ROIs in the 2p stack of a pan-inhibitory sample, and about 13,000 ROIs in the 2p stack of a pan-neuronal sample (Figure 1).



Figure 1. 2p z-stack slabs (11 slices, max projection, about 150 µm below the pia) at the same scale. Left, pan-inhibitory (790322). Right, pan-neuronal (837568).


GFP+ filtering is not needed. For pan-inhibitory samples, GFP+ filtering is necessary to balance the number of candidates between the modalities. For pan-neuronal, that is not necessary anymore: although not all Rn28S+ ROIs have a 2p partner (non-neuronal cells, losing 2p ROIs from vasculature shadows), the density imbalance was small enough to allow using soma-print for matching reliably. Within the bounding box of the final matches, there are 26,789 HCR ROIs (kept by the quality classifier) for 13,074 2p ROIs in 839909, and 30,615 for 14,330 in 837568, about two HCR ROIs per 2p ROI.

title: Automated volumetric multimodal coregistration, Part 2: adapting to pan-neuronal expression
text:
2. Problems with dense data
Dense expression breaks two parts of the Part 1 pipeline. Both come from the same property: with about 10 times as many cells, a local cell arrangement is much less unique.
Axial scale. In Part 1, sz was the peak of an FFT-based correlation between the 2p stack and a side view of the HCR 488 slab. In the dense data the side view is nearly uniform with depth, so the correlation has little to lock onto and plateaus (Figure 2). For an example subject 839909 the peak is just 1.06 times the median (we require 1.10), and its position, 3.30, is far from the value the matched pairs give (2.69).



Figure 2. Correlation sweep for sz in 839909: mean ± s.d. across 5 slabs (each 100 µm thick). The curve is flat above sz ≈ 2.2. Its peak (3.30) is far from the estimate from the matched pairs (2.69).


False positives, mostly at depth. Soma-print compares the arrangement of the nearest neighbors. With dense cells, a wrong partner is much more likely to have a similar-looking neighborhood. This gets worse with depth, for three reasons:

More HCR cells without a 2p partner. 2p detection falls with depth (lower SNR), while HCR density does not. In 839909 there are 2.2–2.3 HCR ROIs per 2p ROI in the upper-middle of the overlap, and 2.7–3.0 in its deepest 200 µm. Each extra HCR cell is another look-alike candidate, and the 2p neighborhoods are more incomplete.
Fewer anchors. The fraction of 2p ROIs matched is 0.96–0.98 between 100 and 250 µm in the 2p stack, 0.87 at 300–350 µm and 0.49 at 350–400 µm. Few anchors at the bottom means the warp there is weakly constrained, and the stack ends beyond the last anchors (section 4).
Axial scale error grows with depth. An error in sz is a position error proportional to depth below the pia. The seed for 839909 (2.90) is 0.21 above the final value (2.69), which is 13 µm at 60 µm below the pia and 63 µm at 300 µm. A misaligned neighborhood is less likely to match its true partner, and more likely to match a look-alike.

Section 3 addresses the first problem and section 4 the second.

title: Automated volumetric multimodal coregistration, Part 2: adapting to pan-neuronal expression
text:
3. Axial scale (sz)
I replaced the sweep with a two-pass estimate:

Seed. sz = HCR layer 1 thickness / 2p layer 1 thickness. Layer 1 has few cells, so the depth where cell density starts to rise marks the L1/L2 boundary in both volumes (Figure 3, panels 1–4). For 839909: 171 µm / 59 µm = 2.90.
Pass 1. Run the matcher with the seed.
Regression. Fit the slope of HCR depth vs 2p depth through the origin, using matched pairs deeper than 30 µm below the pia. This slope is sz (Figure 3, panel 5).

L1/L2 boundary from cell density. In each volume, the ROI centroids are binned by depth and the histogram is smoothed. In the 2p stack the depth is measured from a tilted plane fitted to the tissue (4 µm bins; the tilt that gives the sharpest rise is chosen). In HCR the depth is measured below the pia fitted to the image (6 µm bins, GFP+ ROIs). The steepest rise of the histogram lies inside L2, so starting from there I walk toward the surface until the gradient falls below 25% of its peak; that depth, the foot of the rise, is the L1/L2 boundary. L1 thickness is the boundary minus the pia (Figure 3, panels 1–4).



Figure 3. sz estimation in 839909. Panels 1–2, 2p: side view of the z-stack with the fitted pia and L1/L2 boundary, and the ROI density along depth (L1 = 59 µm). Panels 3–4, HCR: side view (405 channel) and GFP+ ROI density below the pia (L1 = 171 µm). Panel 5, HCR vs 2p depth of matched pairs (10,923 pairs), with the fitted slope through the origin and the seed from the L1 ratio.


The seed only has to be good enough to produce matches over a couple hundreds of microns in 2p zstack in the first pass.

title: Automated volumetric multimodal coregistration, Part 2: adapting to pan-neuronal expression
text:
4. TPS constraint and iteration
The matcher is the same as in Part 1: match, fit a TPS to the accepted pairs, re-warp the 2p cells, repeat. In the first pan-neuronal subject (837568), one deep part of the stack was warped much more than the rest.
The cause is extrapolation. A thin-plate spline fit to the accepted pairs (the anchors) is reliable only inside the region the anchors span. Outside it, the TPS extrapolates, and the extrapolation can shift cells by a large amount. The deepest 2p cells lie just outside that region (few anchors there, section 2), so they were shifted together as one block. As noted in section 2, dense cells make a false-positive group more probable: the shifted block still finds neighbors with similar spacing, so it passes the soma-print and anchor-vote checks (they compare the arrangement of neighbors, not absolute position), and the next TPS fit locks it in. This was not a problem with the sparse pan-inhibitory subjects. The local-flow filter, which would flag it, runs only in round 0.
Two changes fix this:

Bounded TPS. Inside the anchor hull the warp is the exact TPS. Outside it, after a 50 µm margin, the warp blends into a robust global affine fit over 40 µm.
Support gate. A candidate whose 2p position lies outside the hull of the previous round’s accepted anchors (plus 150 µm) cannot become an anchor. In 839909 this removed 62, 500 and 462 candidates in rounds 0, 1 and 2.

Nothing changes inside the hull. When tested this update on the six pan-inhibitory subjects, five gave identical recall and one differed by a single pair (largest recall change 0.003).
Iteration. The iteration process is the same as for sparse sample (pan-inhibitory; Part 1). However, the final polish step described in Part 1 added 974 pairs (9,955 → 10,929), 10% of the pairs, compared to 1.5% in the pan-inhibitory subjects.

title: Automated volumetric multimodal coregistration, Part 2: adapting to pan-neuronal expression
text:
5. Result
In 839909, 10,929 of 13,074 2p ROIs are matched (84%); in 837568, 12,931 of 14,330 (90%). The unmatched ROIs are mostly at the shallowest (mostly due to bad HCR ROI quality) and deepest parts of the stack (mostly due to bad 2p ROI detection from low SNR) (Figure 4, Movie 1, Movie 2). There is no manual ground truth for these subjects, so the results were checked visually.



Figure 4. 2p ROIs by match status in XY, XZ and YZ projections. Top, 837568 (12,931 matched, 1,399 unmatched). Bottom, 839909 (10,929 matched, 2,145 unmatched).





Movie 1. 837568, final registration: warped 2p ROIs swept top-down through the HCR volume. Use the player controls to pause and scrub.




Movie 2. 839909, final registration, same display as Movie 1.

title: Automated volumetric multimodal coregistration
text:
Contributors
The goal of Cell Types and Learning project at the Allen Institute, Neural Dynamics is to link neuronal function to gene expression. This requires accurately matching cells between in vivo functional imaging and ex vivo gene expression data. Traditionally, this was done manually, but the process is difficult to scale. This post is about automating that process.

title: Automated volumetric multimodal coregistration
text:
1. The problem
We record the activity of the same set of neurons across multiple sessions, on average about 20, across 8 different depths in the primary visual cortex. The key to our study is to identify their transcriptomic profiles. We use intermediate in vivo two-photon z-stack imging to link between individual sessions and the final ex vivo HCR volume.



Figure 1. From neuronal activities to cell type. A, two consecutive sessions (N and N+1) of one mouse: mean field of view of each of the 8 planes (target depths 40–320 µm), with ROI outlines colored by the inhibitory subclass of the matched cell. B, the same ROI across sessions (same as in white circles in A) maps to a single cell in the two-photon z-stack, which in turn maps to a single cell in the HCR volume.


The two-photon z-stack covers roughly 400 × 400 x 400 µm of cortex. The HCR volume (cleared, expanded) is about 2.3 × 2.3 mm across and over a millimeter deep, with ~100,000 cells (Figure 2).



Figure 2. Left: max projection of the in vivo 2p GCaMP z-stack (~400 µm). Right: the HCR volume (405 channel, Rn28S) with the true footprint boxed.


The following describes the main challenges in this multimodal coregistration (Figure 3):

Unknown position and orientation. The FOV is roughly targeted at the center of HCR sample (up to ~200 µm from the center of cleared, expanded tissue), and the patch can be rotated (typically ~180° in our setup) and tilted (typically up to ~15°).
Anisotropic expansion. The clearing/expansion step enlarges tissue, and not equally in all directions. From our ground-truth landmarks, depth expands about 1.5× more than the lateral axes.
Non-rigid warping. After the best possible global affine fit, cells are still off by 16–43 µm RMS (up to ~114 µm) — larger than a cell body.
Partial correspondence. Many cells in one volume simply have no partner in the other (segmentation misses, cells that were out of the imaged range).




Figure 3. Ground-truth transformations from the manual coregistration results. A, lateral (XY) vs axial (Z) expansion from 2p to HCR. B, pia tilt of each modality. C, in-plane rotation, as deviation from 180°. D, offset of the 2p volume center from the HCR center. E, the non-rigid residual: landmark mismatch left after the best global anisotropic affine fit (RMS and maximum, in µm).

title: Automated volumetric multimodal coregistration
text:
2. Manual coregistration
(Developed by Omid Zobeiri)
The manual protocol, using BigWarp, goes like this:

Find a constellation of 4–6 cells near the surface of the 2p stack with a distinctive pattern.
Find the matching GFP-positive pattern in the HCR volume. Repeat until you are confident.
Set these as landmarks and apply a thin-plate-spline (TPS) transform.
Expand the set of landmarks with visual pattern matching. Until ~50–100 landmarks to cover the volume.
Use the current warp to propose cell-to-cell matches automatically, then go through every candidate by eye (shape, context, whether accepting it improves local agreement) and add the good ones as new landmarks. Repeat until nothing new appears.

It works, but it is laborious and requires steep learning curve, preventing scaling up. Only 2 people in our institute know how to do it well.

title: Automated volumetric multimodal coregistration
text:
3. Test dataset
We used six subjects with manual ground truth, all with sparse pan-inhibitory GCaMP expression (GCaMP in inhibitory neurons only).
Sparse is convenient: in the 2p stack, each labeled cell is isolated and bright, and in HCR we can find the corresponding cells by their GFP signal. We call those GFP+ cells, and the 2p ↔︎ HCR correspondence lives almost entirely within that population.
Two supporting pieces made everything else possible:

An HCR ROI quality classifier. The HCR segmentation has errors: merged cells, fragments, debris. A LightGBM classifier labels each 3-D ROI as good / bad-but-ok / bad / merged. It’s trained on our own manual labels, uses 405-only features, and reaches a leave-one-subject-out binary AUC of ~0.92. The matcher only considers ROIs the classifier keeps — so it’s a required dependency, not a nicety. Code: capsule-3D-FISH-ROI-classifier (inference), capsule-3D-FISH-ROI-labeling (interactive labeling), and capsule-3D-FISH-ROI-classifier-training (training).
A GFP+ definition. After comparing several options (including pairwise unmixing, which did not help), the most reliable was a Gaussian-mixture fit on the log of 488 spot density per cell.

title: Automated volumetric multimodal coregistration
text:
4. Step 1: rough registration
The initial rough registration is image-based, classical computer vision approach. It required 4 main steps.
(1) Surfaces. We fit the pia (the top surface of the cortex) in both volumes. In each volume, the pia was fit using a 2-D polynomial over the intensity near the top part of the image. In HCR volume, we added iterative reweighted linear squares approach.This gives a common depth coordinate and the relative tilt (up to ~18° between the two).



Figure 4. Pia plane fits over side-view projections, defining depth-from-surface in both volumes.


(2) Lateral scale (sxy). How much bigger does a cell look in HCR than in 2p? We estimated it by comparing the cross-sectional areas of corresponding ROIs (all ROIs in 2p volume, GFP+ ROIs in HCR volume). The median cross-sectional area ratio of the ROIs, square-rooted, gave the lateral scale factor similar to the ground-truth value. Note that this approach cannot be used for estimating axial scale due to difference in z resolution between the two imaging modalities (step 4).



Figure 5. Lateral scale from ROI cross-sectional area. Distributions of the xy bounding-box area of all 2p ROIs (n = 1016) and GFP+ HCR ROIs (n = 3721), with their medians (207 and 669 µm²). The lateral scale is sxy = √(669 / 207) = 1.80, close to the 1.77 obtained from the ground-truth landmarks.


(3) Top-slab 2-D registration. Take a slab beneath the pia from each volume, max-project, and register the 2-D images — trying rigid, affine and piecewise-rigid models and keeping the best by normalized cross-correlation against the raw 488 image. This step was devised from the experience with manual procedure - surface had sparse features for human to match easily, which turns out to be useful for automated procedure as well.



Figure 6. Top-slab 2-D registration. The HCR 488 slab (0–150 µm below the pia) is shown in green and the 2p slab (0–80 µm below the pia) in magenta; overlap appears white. Left to right: the two slabs, their overlay after the rigid fit, and the overlay after piecewise-rigid refinement (NCC 0.09 → 0.18).


(4) Axial scale (sz). We took a side view of the tilt-matched 488 slab, swept sz, and found the peak of the FFT-based correlation. Across the six benchmark subjects the peak matched the ground-truth value exactly.



Figure 7. The axial-scale sweep. Slab-wise FFT correlation between the warped 2p stack and the HCR 488 volume as a function of sz: mean ± s.d. across 5 slabs, each 100 µm thick. The peak (3.10 for this subject) is the chosen scale.


Overlap crop. With pose, scales and depth in hand, we only keep HCR cells that could possibly lie within the 2p volume (plus a 10% margin) — cutting the search space roughly 7×. We made this a binding rule for every later stage: nothing operates outside the overlap crop.
The output of Step 1 is not a final answer. In the ground-truth comparison it’s still tens of microns off in places.

title: Automated volumetric multimodal coregistration
text:
5. Step 2: matching cells with a “soma-print”
Soma-print, from (Wang, Jiang, Sun et al., 2026), was the real breakthrough. Their approach (TRU-FACT) was to align in vivo and ex vivo imaging optically as much as possible, and to use soma-print as ROI matching quantification. Soma-print works great when the initial registration is reasonably accurate (this is the whole reason we needed step 1).
The main idea in our work is to use this as a tool for nonrigid (fine) registration. Main updates in implementation are: (1) making it a 3D version (Figure 8), (2) additional filtering using mutual-best match, local flow coherence, and anchor vote (Movie 1) (3) incorporating it into an iterative refinement loop (inspired from the manual procedure).



Figure 8. The soma-print idea on real geometry: each cell is described by its neighbor-vector constellation, and two cells are compared by their best-matching vector pairs.



Filtering and iterative refinement loop
Soma-print is not a robust matcher when the modalities are not well-aligned (as opposed to how it was used in TRU-FACT). The following steps are designed to improve its reliability in our pipeline:

Wide candidate radius. For each 2p cell, consider all HCR cells within 150 µm — the best soma-print match is often not the nearest neighbor.
Mutual-best. Keep a pair only if each cell is the other’s top choice.
Round-0 local-flow filter. In the first round only, drop pairs whose displacement disagrees with their neighbors’.
Anchor vote. Keep a pair only if at least 3 of its 5 soma-neighbors are also confidently matched.
Fit, warp, repeat. Fit a thin-plate spline to the accepted pairs, re-warp the 2p cells, and match again. Each round improves the warp, and new pairs appear at the edges. On the example subject: 667 → 692 → 698 pairs, then it converges.
Final polish. After the loop converges, rebuild each 2p cell’s descriptor from its 10 nearest accepted pairs, and pair all 2p cells again with the same filters. This added about 1.5% matches.




Movie 1. The customized matcher on real cells: wide candidate search → mutual-best → local-flow filter → anchor vote → iterate with TPS. Use the player controls to pause and scrub.

title: Automated volumetric multimodal coregistration
text:
6. How well does it work?
Against our ground truth, recall is 0.87–0.97 across the six subjects. A part of the loss is due to not having ROI quality filtering in the manual processing (which led to false positives). Precision is more complicated: a number of the “false positives” look like genuine matches missed in the manual process. So our precision numbers are a lower bound.



Figure 9. Final matches on subject 790322 over the HCR 488 projection (698 pairs, 676 of which agree with the independent manual table), and the displacement field that matching + TPS resolved.


And here is the full result — the TPS-warped 2p stack overlaid on the HCR 488 volume, scrolling down from the pia:



Movie 2. Final registration: 2p (magenta) over HCR 488 (cyan), with matched cells accumulating as gold circles. Use the player controls to pause and scrub.

title: Automated volumetric multimodal coregistration
text:
7. Manual QC
As a last step, we added a QC app. It presents matches least-confident-first for pass/fail, lets you add or fix a pair manually with a live re-warp, and exports the final coregistration table. The source repository of the QC app (a Code Ocean interactive capsule) is interactive-capsule-2p-3DFISH-autocoreg-QC.
At least in the 6 subjects we tested, the automated algorithm worked well - manual correction was only at around 10 ROIs out of several hundred per subject.



Figure 10. The QC app GUI.

title: Automated volumetric multimodal coregistration
text:
8. Miscellaneous Notes

This protocol is now used in production in the Allen Institute, for projects across Brain Science and Neural Dynamics.
The same approach was applied to other datasets with similar success (pan-neuronal GCaMP and Xenium - follow up posts).
Prior experience with manual procedure was critical in giving insights to designing the automated pipeline.
Most of the pipeline was developed using Claude Code.

Initial attempt for asking the agent to figure out the solution failed. (Note: main development was done around May 2026.)
Image processing problem seems unique in a sense that a hallucination is easy to check visually. Producing intermediate images for each step helped catch errors early.
Making videos for explaining each step became much easier and fun. It helped communicate the process clearly to others.

We are currently exploring the process to recover more matches (Being led by Matt J. Davis)

The current approach is ROI-to-ROI matching. This depends on the ROI detection quality. ROI detection in the structural z-stack seems to be the main bottleneck. The cause seems to be two-fold: (1) some inactive neurons during the structural z-stack acquisition, and (2) low SNR especially in deeper planes.
By directly registering FOV to HCR, we can recover more matches. We can do this by using chained transformations from FOV to zstack and zstack to HCR.


→ Part 2: pan-neuronal

Code: github.com/jkim0731/2p2fish (the autocoreg package) and github.com/jkim0731/mfish-roi-classifier.

title: Cleaning up optical crosstalk between simultaneously imaged planes in a two-photon mesoscope
text:
DOI
Contributors
Two-photon mesoscopes let us record from a lot of neurons at once, in the Allen Brain Observatory and many other projects across the Institute. One trick for recording even more neurons is to split the laser and image two depths at the same time. It comes with a subtle problem: the two planes bleed into each other.
A faint copy of one plane shows up as “ghost” cells in the other. Left uncorrected, those ghosts look like real neurons. Just as important, the bleed-through contaminates the activity traces (ΔF/F) extracted from genuine ROIs, degrading real cells — not only adding spurious ones.
This post walks through the problem and the correction we run in production: what the crosstalk is and where it comes from, why the obvious fixes don’t work, how our estimator works (minimizing mutual information between the paired planes from the bright ROIs), and how well it does — measured against real ground-truth recordings, against simulations, and against two off-the-shelf alternatives (naive ICA and suite3d). I’ll also cover the quality-control tooling we built to catch the rare failures.

title: Cleaning up optical crosstalk between simultaneously imaged planes in a two-photon mesoscope
text:
1. What is paired-plane crosstalk?
To image more neurons per session, a two-photon mesoscope can be upgraded to capture two depths at once. The excitation laser is split into two beams, one is given a small time delay, and the two are focused at two different depths. We refer to this beam-splitting configuration internally as the multiscope [1].
The multiscope is one of a broader family of temporally-multiplexed two-photon systems — spatiotemporal multiplexing [2], reverberation microscopy [3], and light-beads microscopy [4] — that excite multiple planes and separate them by photon arrival time, and all face the same crosstalk (cf. the Diesel2p mesoscope [5], which uses a separate resonance scanner per beam and so has no comparably structured crosstalk).
Both depths are excited within a single inter-pulse interval (~16 ns at a 62.5 MHz repetition rate), and the fluorescence from each is separated by a time-gated collection window — one gate per plane.
The catch is fluorescence lifetime. A GCaMP molecule keeps emitting for a few nanoseconds after it is excited (the fluorescence lifetime of GFP-based indicators is ≈2.6 ns [6]), so the tail of one plane’s fluorescence spills into the other plane’s collection gate. Those stray photons get counted as the wrong plane’s signal. That is the crosstalk (Figure 1).



Figure 1. Left: one pulse train is split into two beams, offset in time and focused at two depths (the two planes of a “pair”). Right: each pulse’s fluorescence decays over a few ns (τ ≈ 2.6 ns); the tail of one plane is still emitting when the other plane’s collection gate opens, so it is collected as the wrong plane’s signal — bleed-through set by timing and fluorophore lifetime, i.e. the instrument configuration, not the biology.


Because it is optical/temporal, the amount of crosstalk is a property of the acquisition, not of any particular neuron. In a well-tuned and balanced session it is only a few percent — invisible at native contrast, but enough to plant visible ghosts. The clean way to see it is a single-beam recording: image a plane with its own beam only (“clean”), then with both beams on (“crosstalk”). The extra ghost cells that appear in the dual-beam image are the bleed-through (Figure 2).



Figure 2. One plane imaged single-beam (“clean”) vs dual-beam (“crosstalk”). The extra ghost cells that appear in “crosstalk” are the bleed-through from the paired plane. Ground-truth single-beam data from primary visual cortex of a Slc32a1-Cre;TITL2-GCaMP8s (pan-inhibitory) mouse; 100 µm scale bar.

title: Cleaning up optical crosstalk between simultaneously imaged planes in a two-photon mesoscope
section: 2. Why the obvious fixes don’t work
text:
2. Why the obvious fixes don’t work
If crosstalk is just “plane B leaking a fraction of its signal into plane A,” why not estimate that fraction directly — say, regress one plane’s pixel time series against the other’s and subtract? Two confounds get in the way.
The two planes share real biology. They sit at the same location, a little apart in depth, so they see much of the same vasculature shadows and neuropil background. That makes the two images genuinely correlated even with zero crosstalk. Any method that works by making the two planes independent — blind source separation (ICA [7]), or simply minimizing their correlation — is misled by this shared anatomy: minimizing correlation never bottoms out at the right amount and keeps over-subtracting, while ICA’s assumption that the planes are independent is false for genuinely correlated planes, so its coefficient comes out biased — by an amount, and even a direction, that changes with the data (§5).
The two planes don’t move together. You might hope to line the planes up once and just subtract — but a pair does not move as a rigid unit. Each plane is motion-corrected independently, and when we compare the per-frame rigid shifts across 69 hour-long sessions, the two planes of a pair follow visibly different XY trajectories — increasingly so the farther apart in depth they sit (Figure 3).



Figure 3. Paired planes move differently in XY. (a, b) x- and y-shift over one 60-min session for the closest pair (160 & 200 µm, blue) and the furthest-apart pair (40 & 320 µm, red); within a pair, darker = upper plane / lighter = lower. (c) Across all 69 sessions (276 pairs), inter-plane motion divergence over the hour grows with within-pair depth separation (r = 0.45); the exemplar pair is circled.


You can see the consequence directly. Because the planes slide relative to each other, the bleed-through is not pinned to a fixed spot: as you step through a session’s epochs, the ghost cells (a copy of the paired plane) visibly drift across the field of view while the plane’s own cells stay put (Figure 4).



Figure 4. Raw episodic mean FOV of a deep plane stepping through epochs (left), beside the paired plane that is its crosstalk source (right). The faint ghost cells in the raw plane track the bright cells in the paired plane and shift position from epoch to epoch — because the two planes move differently.


Those facts — shared anatomy and a moving, differential offset between planes — are why the correction is built the way it is: work on motion-corrected episodic mean images (instead of signal time series), restrict attention to bright ROIs (to avoid vasculature), and minimize mutual information rather than plain correlation (to account for the shared structure).

title: Cleaning up optical crosstalk between simultaneously imaged planes in a two-photon mesoscope
text:
3. The correction

The model
For a plane A imaged against its partner B, the observed images are a linear mix of the true (crosstalk-free) images:
\[
\begin{bmatrix} \text{imaged}_A \\ \text{imaged}_B \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix} 1-\alpha & \beta \\ \alpha & 1-\beta \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} \text{true}_A \\ \text{true}_B \end{bmatrix}
\]
so α is the fraction of A’s own signal that leaks out into B, and β is the fraction of B that leaks in and contaminates A. Undoing the crosstalk is just inverting this 2×2 mixing matrix. The whole problem is estimating (α, β).
Note this is a relative crosstalk between two planes of different brightness — so the brightness imbalance between the planes matters, and α and β are generally not equal.
Also note that this shares a fundamental principle with ICA; how the two differ in practice is discussed below.
Lastly, applying the inverse mixing matrix not only removes crosstalk signal but also restores the plane’s own signal that was subtracted out by the crosstalk. The correction is therefore a reconstruction of the plane’s own signal, not just a subtraction of the paired plane’s ghost (Figure 7B).


Estimating (α, β)

Work on registered mean images. Each plane is motion-corrected, and the paired plane’s raw movie is registered using the same correction (“registered-to-pair”). This solves the problem of differential motion in XY.
Bright-ROI bounding boxes. Rather than the full frame, the estimator works inside bounding boxes around the brightest ROIs of both planes (Figure 6, left). This avoids the shared low-frequency background — the key to not over-subtracting shared anatomy.
Grid search minimizing mutual information. For each candidate (α, β) on a grid, the estimator unmixes the pair and computes the mutual information (MI) between the two reconstructed images, averaged over the ROI boxes. The chosen (α, β) is the one that minimizes MI — the point at which the two planes carry the least information about each other (Figure 6, right). Using MI rather than correlation matters: correlation falls monotonically as you subtract more, which would reward ever-larger coefficients; MI has a genuine minimum at the right amount.
Averaging for stability. Coefficients are averaged across imaging epochs and across the two directions of a pair (the leak A→B estimated for plane A should equal the leak into B estimated for plane B — see §6), then stored per plane.




Figure 5. The full protocol. Each plane of a pair (signal p1, paired p2) is motion-corrected; each plane’s registration transform is then applied to both planes — its own registered movie and the partner registered-to-pair (the paired plane re-registered with that transform). In each frame the mixing coefficients are estimated by minimizing MI between the two planes; the two estimates (from p1’s and p2’s registration) are averaged, and the inverse mixing matrix is applied to yield the decrosstalked movie for each plane. FOVs at left: dual-beam mean images (old-laser ground truth).





Figure 6. Left: a registered mean FOV plane with the bright-ROI bounding boxes the estimator uses. Right: the normalized-MI landscape over (α, β) for that pair (80 MHz laser ground-truth). The grid search minimum (✚) lands right next to the single-beam ground-truth leak fractions (★) — the objective points at the correct answer.

title: Cleaning up optical crosstalk between simultaneously imaged planes in a two-photon mesoscope
text:
4. Does it work?

How the ground-truth data were collected
To know the true crosstalk we need a recording where one plane’s contribution to the other is known. We get that by blocking one of the two beams: with a beam blocked, its plane is never excited, so whatever appears in that plane’s detector channel is pure crosstalk leaking from the open plane — a dim, scaled replica of the open plane’s image, acquired simultaneously and therefore perfectly co-registered and activity-matched. Regressing the blocked channel onto the open one gives the leak fraction directly, with no estimation and no confound from shared anatomy or motion. Blocking each beam in turn measures both directions of the 2×2 mixing matrix (Figure 7).



Figure 7. How the ground-truth mixing matrix is measured. (A) Block one beam: the un-excited plane’s channel then contains only crosstalk from the open plane — a scaled replica acquired simultaneously. Columns are the two detector channels (ch1 middle, ch2 right); each row blocks one beam, so the signal (open channel) and crosstalk (blocked channel) swap sides. The crosstalk’s intensity range is ~14× smaller, and that ratio is the coefficient (crosstalk ≈ coefficient × signal). α = 0.070 (ch1 → ch2; top row, beam 2 blocked); β = 0.078 (ch2 → ch1; bottom row, beam 1 blocked). (B) Applying the inverse of the mixing matrix built from these ground-truth coefficients to the observed (both-beam) image removes the crosstalk. Observed (left), decrosstalked (middle), and their difference (right; red = crosstalk removed, blue = the plane’s own signal restored by the unmixing). Scale bars 100 µm.




Seeing the correction
On the ground-truth data we can walk a plane through all three states — imaged single-beam (“clean”, the truth), both-beam (“observed”, with crosstalk), and after correction (“decrosstalked”) — for both planes at once (Figure 8). The correction nudges the observed image back toward the clean one; on the high-SNR session mean the change is deliberately subtle (only a few percent of the signal is crosstalk), which is exactly why quality control is hard (§6).



Figure 8. Both planes cycling slowly through single-beam (clean), dual-beam (observed), and decrosstalked. γ-stretched; 100 µm scale bar. Ground-truth data.


The crosstalk is far more striking on a real session when you step through its epochs. Because the two planes move differently (§2), the ghost is not static — it drifts across the field of view over the session. In the raw episodic mean movie below (middle), watch the soft ghost cells in the upper field move in lockstep with the paired plane (right); after decrosstalk (left) they are largely gone while the plane’s own cells stay put.



Figure 9. Episodic-mean FOV stepping through epochs: decrosstalked (left) and raw (middle) — raw placed next to the paired plane (right, the crosstalk source, re-registered with this plane’s registration transform). A real 60-min session, the furthest-apart pair (planes 6–7; depths 304 µm and 37 µm, top-right), β ≈ 0.08. Raw and decrosstalked share one contrast window; the paired plane has its own. The moving ghost cells that track the paired plane are removed by the correction.


It also works in dense GCaMP8 samples. Everything above is sparse pan-inhibitory data. In pan-neuronal soma-targeting recordings (SNAP25-Cre;TITL2-RiboL1-GCaMP8s), far more cells are labeled. The dense paired plane casts a correspondingly dense ghost into its partner, and — because the planes move differently — that ghost drifts across epochs; the same estimator removes it (Figure 10).



Figure 10. A dense pan-neuronal plane (SNAP25-Cre;TITL2-RiboL1-GCaMP8s) stepping through epochs: decrosstalked (left), raw (middle), and the paired plane that is the crosstalk source (right; depths 79 µm and 283 µm, top-right). Raw and decrosstalked share one contrast window; the paired plane has its own. The moving bleed-through from the dense paired plane is removed by the correction. 100 µm scale bar.


The removed structure is exactly the paired plane’s cells — the crosstalk — and nothing else. But “looks clean” is not a measurement. For that we need ground truth.

title: Cleaning up optical crosstalk between simultaneously imaged planes in a two-photon mesoscope
section: 5. How accurate is it? Ground truth, simulation, and a bake-off
text:
5. How accurate is it? Ground truth, simulation, and a bake-off
The single-beam ground-truth recordings give us the true leak fractions directly (regress the blocked channel on the open channel within ROIs): 0.070 / 0.078 for the 80 MHz laser and 0.029 / 0.027 for the 62.5 MHz laser. That lets us score any estimator by how close its (α, β) come to the truth, and by how much signal↔︎paired dependence is left after unmixing. We compared three estimators:



estimator
idea




production
minimize normalized MI over bright-ROI boxes


naive ICA
FastICA blind source separation


suite3d
correlation-inflection estimator [8] (code)



For a fair comparison, all three estimators were run on the exact same bright-ROI boxes, so the test isolates the estimator itself.
On the real ground-truth data, production essentially nails it. Its (α, β) sit right on the ground-truth values (Figure 11), its mean coefficient error is 0.007, and it drives the residual signal↔︎paired correlation from the raw ceiling (0.465) down to 0.189 — i.e. to the shared-anatomy floor (0.186). It removes essentially all the removable crosstalk.



Figure 11. Estimated (α, β) vs the single-beam ground truth (★). Production (●) overlaps the truth for both lasers; naive ICA is close on the 80 MHz laser but drifts on the low-crosstalk 62.5 MHz laser; suite3d under-shoots to ~0.01.


On simulations — impose a known (α, β) on the clean images (a full 2-D grid, not just the α = β diagonal) and try to recover it — the same picture holds across the whole plane (Figure 12). Production’s estimates land right on the true grid points; naive ICA is systematically biased — over-estimating on the 80 MHz laser and under-estimating on the low-crosstalk 62.5 MHz laser; and suite3d collapses to ≈0.01 regardless of the true value, ignoring the signal almost entirely.



Figure 12. (a, b) Recovered vs true (α, β) across the 2-D simulation grid, one panel per laser: each line runs from a true grid point (✚) to a method’s estimate. Production (blue) sits on the grid; naive ICA (orange) is biased (over on the 80 MHz laser, under on 62.5 MHz); suite3d (green) fans to ≈0.01. (c) Mean absolute coefficient error per method and laser (± std over the grid, log axis): production ≈ 0.002–0.004, naive ICA ≈ 0.010–0.029, suite3d ≈ 0.11–0.12.


Takeaway from the bake-off. All three methods were fit on identical bright-ROI patches, so the comparison isolates the estimator. The ranking is production > naive ICA > suite3d, and production is the only method that reliably reaches the shared-anatomy floor. suite3d’s correlation-inflection point [8] was likely intended to separate genuine shared correlation from crosstalk — i.e., to cope with the shared anatomy — but it consistently under-corrected. When tested on the real data at the full frame, it corrected somewhat but still under-corrected in most cases.

title: Cleaning up optical crosstalk between simultaneously imaged planes in a two-photon mesoscope
text:
6. Quality control
Across a large pan-inhibitory dataset, most planes are corrected well — but a few are not, and the failures are easy to miss. We built two QC tools.
An interactive visual-QC app (Figure 13) lets a labeler flip PRE↔︎POST and toggle the paired (crosstalk-source) view at matched contrast, scrub epochs, and label each plane good / under-corrected / over-corrected / unsure. These human labels are the ground truth the automatic metrics are validated against.



Figure 13. The Qt desktop QC app: control panel (session/pair/epoch navigation, α/β readout, per-plane label buttons) and two plane panes. Space flips PRE↔︎POST; p toggles the paired view.


Automatic QC checks exploit two structural facts about a correct estimate (Figure 14):

The MI landscape is stable across epochs and has one well-located minimum. If the per-epoch landscapes wander or the minimum is multi-modal, the estimate is untrustworthy. In practice the minimum barely moves (σ ≈ 0.005–0.02).
Reciprocity. A physical leak between planes p and q is estimated twice: the leak p→q appears as α of plane p and as β of plane q. For a sound estimate these agree (α_p ≈ β_q); a large reciprocity gap flags a one-plane segmentation or registration breakdown that per-plane views miss. Median gap ≈ 0.01.




Figure 14. The per-plane QC page: per-epoch MI landscapes (top), argmin stability and α/β-vs-epoch (middle), and pair reciprocity (bottom, α_p vs β_q with a 0.05 flag).


One important lesson from QC: judge decrosstalk on individual epochs, not the session mean. Decrosstalk is a linear, per-frame operation, so the corrected session-mean is exactly the average of the corrected epochs — and the high-SNR mean can camouflage residual crosstalk that individual, lower-SNR epochs expose. A plane whose mean looks perfectly clean can still show per-epoch artifacts.

title: Cleaning up optical crosstalk between simultaneously imaged planes in a two-photon mesoscope
text:
Summary
Paired-plane crosstalk in a beam-splitting mesoscope is an optical/temporal artifact — a few-percent ghost of one depth plane bleeding into the other. Because the two planes share real anatomy and don’t move in lockstep, naive decorrelation over-subtracts. Estimating the mixing coefficients by minimizing mutual information inside bright ROIs on registered mean images sidesteps both confounds, and — validated against single-beam ground truth, simulations, and two alternative estimators — removes essentially all removable crosstalk, reaching the irreducible shared-anatomy floor and clearly beating naive ICA and suite3d. QC tooling catches the rare failures.
